Prediction: Most of economics asks causal questions. Jon Kleinberg, Jens Ludwig, Sendhil Mullainathan and Ziad Obermeyer pointed out that many policy decisions do not. A farmer wondering whether a rain dance brings rain needs a causal effect. A person deciding whether to take an umbrella needs only a forecast: the umbrella does not change the weather. Mullainathan and Jann Spiess put it as y-hat problems against beta-hat problems. Bail is an umbrella problem: the judge needs to know whether this person will come back. So is a hip replacement, whose benefit comes over years, for a patient who may not live that long. So are inspections: which restaurant, which building, which tax return. Each is a decision whose value turns on a prediction, and prediction is what machine learning does best.

The Island has bail courts too: 40,000 defendants, fifty judges, each case assigned at random. Split them in half: one half to learn from, the other to test on. The algorithm can learn only from the defendants the judges released, because only their outcomes are seen. It is a random forest: many decision trees, each grown on a resample, each split chosen to separate those who came back from those who did not, using age, prior arrests, missed court dates, the charge and whether the person has a job. On the test half, group defendants by their predicted risk, in tenths, and compare with the truth the simulation knows. The forest ranks them well, but it underestimates the riskiest tenth: it learned from the released, who were the less risky of their kind. Remember that for chapter three.

Called it? In 1954 the psychologist Paul Meehl reviewed every study he could find that pitted clinicians against simple statistical rules applied to the same facts, and concluded that the rules did as well or better. Experts are inconsistent, and they give weight to vivid details. In 2000 William Grove and colleagues pooled 136 such studies. The mechanical rule was about ten percent more accurate on average, much better in a third to nearly half of the studies, and much worse in a few. The verdict: right. With one caveat this part keeps returning to: the expert sometimes sees what the records do not.
PlayIt: Chapter two. Play it: ten cases.

Your turn. One morning in the Island's court, ten defendants, and room in the jail for three. You see what the judge's file shows: age, prior arrests, how many court dates they have missed before, the charge, and whether they have a job. The law asks one thing: who is least likely to come back to court? Remember that the charge is about the past, not about coming back. Which three would you detain?

Here is what lay behind the files. Under each defendant, the algorithm's predicted chance of failing to appear, what the judge did, and the true chance the Island knows. The algorithm detains A, C, D: the youngest, with the most missed court dates. On average, detaining them prevents 1.98 failures to appear. The judge detained C, E, J, 3 of them charged with violence, which on the Island says little about coming back: 1.02 failures prevented. The best possible three would prevent 1.98. How did your three do? Add up their true chances. The judge is not foolish: the charge is vivid, and the law cares about it in other ways. But for this one question, the record of missed dates is what predicts.
Labels: Here is the choice the court faces, on the test half. The blue curve: detain the share of defendants with the highest predicted risk, and count the failures to appear among everyone else. Detain more, fewer failures. The pink points are the judges, grouped by how lenient they are, and the white point is all of them together: 28 percent detained, 8.4 failures per hundred defendants. At the judges' detention rate, the algorithm's ranking has 18 percent fewer failures. Or, for the judges' failure rate, it detains 30 percent fewer people. But this picture cheats. It uses what every detained defendant would have done if released, which the Island knows and no real court ever does.

The way round it is a design, not a model. Because cases go to judges at random, every judge sees the same kind of defendant. Take the most lenient fifth of the judges. Among the defendants they released, let the algorithm detain more, highest predicted risk first, until as many are detained as a stricter group of judges detained. Every failure among those still released was actually observed, because the lenient judges released them. This is the contraction design. Compare: at each stricter group's detention rate, the algorithm's contracted caseload has fewer failures than those judges' own, using no outcome that was never seen.

Why not simply fill in the missing outcomes with the algorithm's own predictions? That shortcut says the algorithm would see 6.3 failures per hundred at the judges' detention rate. The truth is 6.9. The gap comes from what the judges saw in court and the records do not: on the Island, a signal that the judges used and the algorithm cannot. The defendants they detained were riskier than their records suggest: 24 percent in truth, 16 percent by the model. So the shortcut flatters the algorithm. Kleinberg and his coauthors relied instead on the random assignment of judges, the instrument idea of Part four: lenient and strict judges see the same kind of defendant.
Causation: Chapter four. Prediction is not causation.

Prediction is the right tool when the decision does not change the outcome. Most policies are meant to change it. The Island has a job programme with places for a fifth of its unemployed. Who should get them? A natural answer: predict who is most likely to stay out of work, and start there. But look at the programme's effect, which the Island knows, by risk. People likely to find work anyway gain little. And people far from any job gain little too: a few weeks of training do not bridge that distance. The effect is largest in the middle. The most at risk are not the most helped.

Now give out the places four ways and count the people kept out of unemployment per hundred places. At random: 14. To the highest predicted risk: 7, worse than at random. To the people with the largest effect, as estimated by a causal forest from a randomized trial: 25. And to the largest true effect, which no one ever knows: 31. A perfect forecast of who will stay unemployed would not help here. Targeting needs effects, and effects need experiments, which chapter six returns to.

Even when prediction is the right tool, what you predict is a choice. Ziad Obermeyer, Brian Powers, Christine Vogeli and Sendhil Mullainathan studied an algorithm used by a large health system to pick patients for extra care. It predicted each patient's future medical costs. Costs are not needs. Less was spent on Black patients with the same illnesses, so at the same score they were sicker. Changing the label from costs to a measure of health would raise the share of Black patients among those flagged from 17.7 percent to 46.5. The algorithm predicted costs very well. It was the wrong target.
DML: Machine learning predicts; most of economics wants a causal effect. Can the two be combined? Take the partially linear model. The outcome is theta times a treatment, plus some function g of background variables; and the treatment itself depends on those variables through another function, m. Theta, here one, is what we want. g and m are nuisances: we do not care about them, but we must get them right enough. On the Island they are curved, with interactions and thresholds, and they share variables, so the treatment is confounded. Ordinary least squares with the controls entered linearly misses the curves, and the bias stays. Replacing g with a machine-learning fit, and regressing what is left of y on d, sounds like the fix. It is not, because the learner's own errors are correlated with d.

Draw 50 samples of 1,500 from the Island and estimate theta four ways. Each dot is one sample. With no controls: about 1.53, the confounding unchecked. With the controls entered linearly: 1.48, hardly better. With a machine-learning fit plugged in naively: 1.17, closer, and still clearly wrong. With double machine learning: 1.01, centred on the truth, and its ninety percent intervals cover the truth in 86 percent of samples.

Two ideas make it work. First, orthogonality. Partial the controls out of both the outcome and the treatment, then regress residual on residual, as Peter Robinson did for kernel estimators in 1988. The learners' errors then enter only as a product, so modest errors in each become a negligible error in theta. Second, cross-fitting: fit the learners on one part of the sample and use them on another, then swap, so a learner never grades its own homework. What it buys: any reasonably accurate learner for the nuisances, forests, boosting, the lasso or a network, and an ordinary standard error for theta. What it does not buy is a design. If a confounder is missing from X, double machine learning is exactly as biased as least squares.
Forests: Chapter six. Heterogeneous effects and policy learning.

To target by effects, you have to estimate them, person by person, and they are never observed: nobody is both treated and untreated. In gold, the effect the Island knows, by risk. Start from a randomized trial: on the Island, 4,000 unemployed people, half given a place at random. Stefan Wager and Susan Athey's causal forest grows trees that split where the effect differs, not where the outcome does. And it is honest: one half of each tree's sample chooses the splits and the other half estimates the effect in each leaf, so the forest cannot fit its own noise. Averaged by risk, the forest's estimates follow the true hump, flattened at the edges where data are thin.

Now the allocation, for every size of programme. Places at random: the gain grows in proportion. By risk: less than at random until a third of the unemployed have places. By the forest's estimated effect: close to the best possible, which uses the true effects. Choosing a rule this way is policy learning, after Toru Kitagawa and Aleksey Tetenov and after Athey and Wager: pick, from a class of simple rules, the one with the largest estimated gain, and bound how much worse than the best it can be. Simple rules matter: a programme officer has to be able to apply them, and a citizen to understand them.
Text: Chapter seven. Text and images as data.

Much of what economists care about was never written down as a number. It sits in newspapers, meeting minutes, company filings and reviews; the words can be counted, or turned into vectors that place similar meanings near each other; a model trained on a few hundred documents labelled by hand can then label millions. Matthew Gentzkow, Bryan Kelly and Matt Taddy surveyed the methods: measures of policy uncertainty, of a central bank's tone, of the risks firms say they face, of politicians' slant. Images work the same way. Neal Jean and coauthors trained a network on satellite pictures to predict consumption in villages in five African countries, explaining up to three quarters of its variation, where surveys are rare.

But a predicted label is a measurement with error, and the error does not average away. On the Island, 20,000 news articles, 12 percent about layoffs. A good classifier catches 90 percent of them and wrongly flags 4 percent of the rest. Its estimate of the share is 14.3 percent, every time, with a confident interval that never covers the truth. Labelling a random four hundred by hand is unbiased, but noisy: plus or minus 2.7 points. Prediction-powered inference, from Anastasios Angelopoulos and colleagues, uses both: the classifier's share on everything, corrected by its average error on the hand-labelled four hundred. Unbiased, covering the truth 90 percent of the time, and a third narrower than the hand labels alone. The same idea works for regressions whose outcome is a prediction.
Deep: Chapter eight. Deep learning as a solution method.

Machine learning can also solve models. Take Part twenty's growth model in its simplest form: log utility, capital that wears out in a year. Each year output, k to the alpha, is split between consumption and next year's capital, by a saving rate s that may depend on k. The optimal rule satisfies the Euler equation at every k. So represent s by a small neural network, capital in, a saving rate out, and train it to make the Euler equation hold on sixty-four capital stocks, with the series' own automatic differentiation computing the gradients. William Brock and Leonard Mirman found the answer by hand in 1972: save alpha times beta, 0.3135, whatever k is. The network does not know that.

Train it. On the left, the squared Euler error, falling by seven orders of magnitude. On the right, the rule the network has learned, at the start, after fifty steps, after two hundred, and at the end, against Brock and Mirman's answer in gold. The learned rule is flat at alpha times beta, within 0.00003 everywhere on the grid. The network found the closed form without being told it.

Why do this when a grid would do? Because a grid needs a point for every combination of states, and the count explodes: ten state variables with ten points each is ten billion points. A network's cost grows far more slowly. That reaches the economies of Part fifty-two, with many kinds of household, portfolios and several shocks: Marlon Azinovic, Luca Gaegauf and Simon Scheidegger's deep equilibrium nets, and the methods of Lilia and Serguei Maliar and Pablo Winant. The checks are the old ones: Euler errors off the training points, simulated paths, and a case with a known answer, like this one. The risks are new: no guarantee of the global optimum, and errors that hide where the economy rarely goes.
Agents: Part forty-four put two learning algorithms in charge of prices. Here they are again, in 8 sessions. Each is a Q-learner: it tries prices, keeps a table of how well each did after each pair of last prices, and slowly stops experimenting. They never communicate. In almost every session they settle well above the competitive price, most of the way to monopoly: a profit gain of 0.78 on average. Emilio Calvano, Giacomo Calzolari, Vincenzo Denicolò and Sergio Pastorello showed why: the learned strategies punish a rival who undercuts, so undercutting does not pay. Nobody programmed collusion; it was learned. Whether the law can reach it is Part forty-four's open question.

Learning agents are also a laboratory. Stephan Zheng and coauthors' AI Economist trains a planner to choose a tax schedule while the simulated workers it taxes learn how much to work, build and trade. No closed form is needed, the agents can be as rich as the simulation allows, and the planner adapts to how they respond. The caution: the agents learn what the simulation rewards. Real people bring habits and rules of thumb, Part forty-five's biases, and politics, that no simulation was trained on. So it is a laboratory for mechanisms, beside theory and experiments, not a replacement for either.
Fairness: In 2016 the newsroom ProPublica studied a commercial risk score used for more than ten thousand defendants in Broward County, Florida. Among defendants who did not go on to reoffend, Black defendants had been labelled higher risk forty-five percent of the time, white defendants twenty-three percent. The company replied that at each score, Black and white defendants reoffended at about the same rate: the score meant the same thing for both. Both were true. When two groups have different rates of the outcome, no score can satisfy both definitions of fairness at once.

The Island shows why with the best score possible: each defendant's true risk. Two groups: in A, 24 percent would fail to appear; in B, 37 percent, perhaps because B's neighbourhoods are policed more heavily, so its records are longer. Detain anyone whose score is above 0.3. The score is perfectly calibrated: at every level, the share who fail is the same in both groups. Now the errors. Of those who would have come back, 22 percent of group A are detained, and 48 percent of group B. Of those who would not, 48 percent of A are released, and 22 percent of B. A perfectly accurate, perfectly calibrated score, and the errors still fall differently on the two groups.

Alexandra Chouldechova wrote the reason in one line. The false positive rate equals the odds of the outcome in the group, times a term in the positive predictive value, times one minus the false negative rate. If two groups differ in their base rates and the score means the same thing in both, the error rates must differ. Jon Kleinberg, Sendhil Mullainathan and Manish Raghavan proved the general version: calibration and equal error rates for both kinds of error cannot hold together, except with equal base rates or perfect prediction. Which errors matter more, a wrongful detention or a missed court date, is a value judgement. Economics can price the trade-off and show who bears it; it cannot settle it. And the base rates themselves may carry the history of how each group was policed.
Dials: Chapter thirteen. The Dials: algorithms against judges.

This part opens one Dial: how much an algorithm's ranking adds to a judge's decision, measured as the fall in the outcome the decision is meant to prevent, at the same detention rate. Kleinberg and his coauthors in New York City: up to 0.25, about a quarter. The Island, where the truth is known: 0.18. And the Island again, by the contraction design, using only outcomes that were seen: 0.15 to 0.17, a little below the truth, because contraction can only detain more of the lenient judges' released, not release anyone they jailed. The status: depends on the setting. Where the decision is a prediction and the records carry most of the signal, the gains are large. Where the judge sees what the records do not, they shrink, and only a design that copes with selective labels can tell.
Frontier: Chapter fifteen. Frontier: foundation models for economic data.

The frontier begins where this part's hook ended: the judge sees things the records do not. Rerun the Island's courts with the courtroom signal made weaker or stronger. If judges see nothing extra, the algorithm prevents 24 percent of failures at their detention rate; at this part's setting, 18. As the signal grows, the advantage shrinks, and then reverses: when the judge sees enough, ranking by the records alone makes things worse. So the research question is not machine against human but how to combine them: which cases to hand over, when a person should defer, and why, in experiments with doctors and other experts, people often weigh the machine's advice badly.

What remains open? Foundation models for economic data: networks pretrained on millions of firms' accounts, prices or job histories, then tuned to a question, the way language models are tuned to a task. Automated structural estimation: networks that learn, by simulation, the map from data to a model's parameters, as Part fifty-four's amortized estimator did, for models too slow to estimate any other way. Agents in markets: pricing, bidding and negotiating algorithms that learn from each other, and what competition policy owes them. And the old questions, which no amount of data removes: what would have happened otherwise, and who decided what was measured.
